screens.title: Monitoring and Troubleshooting Edge Services
screens.narratorSegment: In this lesson you will learn how to gain consistent visibility into AWS edge services and how to diagnose the most common issues. We focus on three pillars: the metrics and logs CloudFront exports to CloudWatch and S3, the DNS health checks and query logs for Route 53, and the endpoint metrics Global Accelerator provides. I will show you what metrics to watch, how to interpret access logs, and the typical misconfigurations that cause stale content, DNS failures, and endpoint outages. You’ll also learn a troubleshooting workflow: detect with a metric alarm, investigate with logs and health checks, confirm with targeted tests, and remediate with configuration changes or cache invalidation. For example, a sudden drop in CloudFront CacheHitRatio usually points to cache-key changes such as forwarding all query strings; the right fix is to adjust cache policies and validate via CloudWatch. By the end you’ll understand which alarms to create, what logs to inspect, and how to prioritize fixes for global user impact. Think about how you would spot an origin error in CloudWatch and what sequence of checks would give you a quick root cause.

First, you will identify the key metrics for CloudFront, Route 53, and Global Accelerator and know why each matters. Second, you will use CloudWatch, CloudTrail, and access logs as an investigative toolkit: set alarms, inspect A P I changes, and parse access logs for request patterns. Third, you will diagnose and resolve common CloudFront issues such as stale content and origin errors by applying cache policy checks, invalidation, and certificate verification. As you progress you should be able to create alarms, analyze logs, reproduce a cache hit ratio drop, and choose the correct remediation for DNS or endpoint faults. These skills reduce downtime and improve user experience for globally distributed applications.

screens.title: CloudFront Metrics — what to watch
screens.narratorSegment: CloudFront exports several metrics to CloudWatch that directly show distribution behavior and performance. Define each metric in simple terms and learn why it matters. Requests counts total viewer traffic and helps you detect traffic spikes. BytesDownloaded shows bandwidth usage and billing impact. CacheHitRatio is the percentage of requests served from edge caches; a low ratio usually means the cache key is too specific or TTLs are too short. OriginLatency measures how long CloudFront waits for content from the origin, pointing to origin performance or network issues. OriginErrorRate and 4xx/5xx error rates indicate failures at the origin or client problems. Concretely, if CacheHitRatio drops from 98% to 40% after a config change, inspect whether query strings or headers were added to the cache key. A common misconception is to blame the origin before checking cache policy — often the policy change is the root cause. Example: a static site that previously served the same asset for all users will begin missing the cache when the distribution starts forwarding all headers. Takeaway: pick a small set of metrics to monitor, set alarms for significant deviations, and pair metric anomalies with access-log inspection to confirm the cause. How will you choose thresholds that signal real problems without noise?

content.html:
Module 12 › Chapter 11.10 › CloudFront Metrics
Definition
Core CloudFront metrics
  • Requests: total viewer requests, surface traffic spikes.
  • BytesDownloaded: bandwidth used by viewers.
  • CacheHitRatio: percent served from cache; low ratio often signals cache-key or TTL issues.
  • OriginLatency: time to fetch from origin; high values suggest origin or network bottlenecks.
  • OriginErrorRate / 4xx / 5xx: indicate failed origin responses or client errors.
Takeaway
Key Takeaway

Track cache and origin metrics together. A cache drop plus normal origin latency suggests cache-key changes; a cache drop plus high origin latency suggests origin problems.

Example & common mistake
Example scenario
After a deployment you see CacheHitRatio drop from 98% to 40% while OriginLatency remains low. Investigation shows the cache policy was changed to forward all query strings. Fix: restore optimized cache policy and monitor recovery.
Pro-tip
Set an alarm for CacheHitRatio with a short evaluation period, but require multiple data points to avoid false positives.
Check your understanding
If OriginErrorRate spikes and cache ratio is stable, is the origin or the cache likelier the problem? (Answer: origin.)

screens.title: CloudFront Access Logs
screens.narratorSegment: CloudFront access logs provide a detailed record of every request, delivered to an S3 bucket for analysis. Logs include the viewer IP, date/time, HTTP method and URI, status code, bytes transferred, cache result fields like x-edge-result-type and x-edge-response-result-type, referrer, user agent, and TLS details. These fields tell you if an edge returned a Hit or Miss and help correlate user complaints with concrete requests. A practical investigation starts by searching for many Miss entries using Athena or by downloading a sample log to inspect. For example, find lines with x-edge-result-type: Miss and then check the query strings or headers in those requests; if they differ widely, forwarding query strings is a likely cause. A common misunderstanding is to treat all Misses as origin failure; many are simply cache-key mismatches. Here’s an example log excerpt to inspect for Miss entries and query parameters. When you parse logs, group by URI and cache result to spot patterns, then validate cache policy and invalidate if a quick fix is needed. How will you use logs to prove whether a config change or user behavior caused the miss pattern?

content.html:
Module 12 › Chapter 11.10 › CloudFront Access Logs
Log anatomy
  • Viewer IP: locate affected client regions.
  • Date/Time, Method, URI: reproduce the request.
  • Status & Bytes: detect errors or heavy transfers.
  • x-edge-result-type: Hit vs Miss classification.
  • TLS fields: diagnose certificate or protocol issues.
Common mistake
Assuming 'Miss' equals origin failure. Often a Miss results from a changed cache key or forwarded query strings; check request URI and query parameters first.
Example excerpt
2026-09-01 12:02:33 ABCDE12345 example.com GET /index.html?rand=123 200 1024 "-" "Mozilla/5.0" Miss 0.002 x-edge-response-result-type:Miss
Investigation
Filter for x-edge-result-type:Miss and group by query string to find whether unique parameters cause misses.
Next step
If many unique query parameters appear, review cache policy for unnecessary forwarded query strings and revert or tighten policy.

screens.title: Fixing stale content and cache invalidation
screens.narratorSegment: Stale content is a frequent issue when CloudFront serves older objects despite the origin being updated. Start by checking the Cache-Control headers from the origin and the CloudFront cache policy. CloudFront respects origin headers unless a distribution's Minimum TTL overrides them; that override is a common cause of stale content. A practical troubleshooting sequence: first, confirm the origin recently updated the object by fetching it directly from the origin. Next, check CloudFront metrics for CacheHitRatio and CloudFront access logs for x-edge-result-type to see if requests are served from cache. If the Minimum TTL is longer than the origin max-age, CloudFront will retain the old object; correction is to lower Minimum TTL or invalidate the object. Invalidations force edge caches to fetch fresh content immediately using the create-invalidation A P I. Use invalidation sparingly because it costs and creates load on the origin. A misconception is to immediately make the bucket public or change the viewer protocol; these rarely fix cache freshness. Example: if Cache-Control: max-age=3600 is set but Minimum TTL is 86400, CloudFront keeps serving the cached object for a day. The takeaway: align origin headers and cache policy, and use invalidation as a controlled remediation.

keyIdea.text: Align origin Cache-Control and CloudFront Minimum TTL; use invalidation when you need immediate refresh but consider cost and origin load.

content.html:
Module 12 › Chapter 11.10 › Stale Content & Invalidation
Definition
Stale content occurs when CloudFront serves cached objects that no longer match the origin. Key controls are origin Cache-Control headers and CloudFront cache policy Minimum TTL. If Minimum TTL exceeds the origin max-age, CloudFront will ignore the newer origin object until the edge TTL expires.
Step-by-step remediation
  1. Confirm origin holds the updated object by requesting origin URL directly.
  2. Check CloudFront cache policy Minimum TTL vs origin Cache-Control.
  3. If policy enforces longer TTL, update cache policy or use invalidation for immediate fix.
  4. Monitor CacheHitRatio and access logs to confirm recovery.
Concrete example
Example
Origin sets Cache-Control: max-age=3600 but CloudFront Minimum TTL is 86400. Users see old content for up to a day. Fix by lowering Minimum TTL to match or using create-invalidation to clear the object.
Command
Use the invalidation API to force refresh: create-invalidation with the path of the stale object.
Key takeaway
Prefer aligning headers and policy; invalidate only when immediate refresh is required.

screens.title: Origin Errors and 403 from S3
screens.narratorSegment: Origin errors manifest as elevated OriginErrorRate or increased 5xx responses in CloudFront metrics. The practical first step is to correlate CloudFront's error spikes with origin logs — ALB, EC2 or S3 logs — and CloudWatch metrics for the origin. A 5xx spike usually means the origin is failing to respond or returning errors due to application issues or overload. A 403 from an S3 origin is often a permissions or Origin Access Control problem: ensure the CloudFront-generated bucket policy is present and that the bucket is not publicly accessible while allowing CloudFront to fetch. A common misconception is that 403 always means the object is missing; missing objects typically return 404. Instead, 403 indicates access denied. Example: after enabling OAC, you forget to update the S3 bucket policy; CloudFront starts receiving 403s even though objects exist. To fix this, review the bucket policy and ensure the CloudFront OAC identity has read access. Always validate TLS certificates and viewer protocol policy separately if you see HTTPS errors. Ending question: when you see increased OriginErrorRate, what two logs will you inspect first to separate origin failures from edge configuration problems?

keyIdea.title: Error diagnosis
keyIdea.text: Use origin logs plus CloudFront metrics to separate application errors and permission issues like S3 403s; check OAC and bucket policy for S3 origins.

content.html:
Module 12 › Chapter 11.10 › Origin Errors vs Permissions
Comparison
5xx Origin Failures
Cause: application errors, resource exhaustion, bad origin config. Check origin logs and CPU/memory metrics on the origin.
403 from S3
Cause: permission or OAC misconfiguration. Verify bucket policy and the CloudFront origin access identity or OAC association.
Concrete checks
  • Inspect CloudFront OriginErrorRate and 5xx metrics in CloudWatch.
  • Tail origin logs (ALB, EC2, ECS) to find application stack traces or permission denials.
  • For S3, confirm the CloudFront OAC identity is allowed in the bucket policy; avoid making the bucket public.
Example
After enabling OAC, CloudFront returns 403 even though objects exist. The bucket policy lacks the new OAC principal. Add the OAC identity to the bucket policy to restore access.

screens.title: Route 53 health checks and query logs
screens.narratorSegment: Route 53 health checks are fundamental for automated failover and reliable routing. A health check periodically probes an endpoint and reports Healthy or Unhealthy. If a health check flips to Unhealthy, failover or routing decisions may change — so monitor these states and configure thresholds appropriately. In addition to health checks, Route 53 can deliver query logs to CloudWatch or S3; query logs record DNS requests seen by the hosted zone and can reveal querying patterns, sources of resolution failure, or misrouted clients. A practical diagnostic starts with running dig or nslookup from different regions to confirm whether records resolve consistently. If failover does not trigger, verify that the health check targets the correct endpoint, that the request path returns the expected status, and that the thresholds for consecutive failures are not too permissive. A common misconception is that DNS propagation is instantaneous; TTL influences global visibility and can delay changes. Example: a failover didn't trigger because the health check used the wrong path and always returned 200 but with unexpected content; correct the path and adjust thresholds. The takeaway: health checks and query logs together provide both state and transactional evidence for DNS troubleshooting.

keyIdea.text: Use health check status for routing decisions and query logs to audit resolution traffic; confirm endpoints with dig across regions when troubleshooting.

content.html:
Module 12 › Chapter 11.10 › Route 53 Health Checks
Definition
Health checks periodically probe endpoints and report state. They are used by Route 53 to make failover and routing decisions. Query logs capture DNS queries for hosted zones and are useful for auditing and troubleshooting resolution problems.
Checklist
  • Is the health check targeting the right host and path?
  • Are thresholds for unhealthy status appropriate to avoid flapping?
  • Are private hosted zones associated with the correct VPCs for hybrid DNS?
Example & troubleshooting
If failover does not trigger, run dig from multiple regions to see if the record resolves and inspect the health check status. A health check that uses the wrong URL path may return 200 but still be functionally invalid for failover.
Pro-tip
Use shorter TTLs for records you expect to update frequently, but be mindful of increased query volume.
Check
For private zones, verify VPC associations and that network connectivity (Direct Connect/VPN) is active for hybrid resolution.

screens.title: Global Accelerator metrics and endpoint health
screens.narratorSegment: Global Accelerator reports metrics that show endpoint health and traffic through the accelerator. HealthyEndpointCount and UnhealthyEndpointCount tell you whether endpoints in an endpoint group are considered reachable; a drop in the healthy count will divert traffic according to your configuration. BytesIn and BytesOut measure throughput across the accelerator, and ActiveFlowCount measures concurrent network flows, which can indicate surge traffic. When you see UnhealthyEndpointCount increasing, check the underlying ALB, NLB, or EC2 health checks and security groups. A common source of problems is a health check configuration mismatch: Global Accelerator relies on the same targets that ALB/NLB use, and if those targets are failing or blocked by security group rules, Global Accelerator will mark endpoints unhealthy. Example: traffic stops reaching Europe because the region's ALB returns unhealthy; the correct next step is to inspect the ALB target health and instance metrics for that region. Misconception: assuming Global Accelerator health alone pinpoints the problem — you must check the resource beneath the accelerator. Takeaway: use HealthyEndpointCount with direct checks on ALBs/NLBs and security groups to restore reachability quickly. Global Accelerator metrics and endpoint health means use healthyendpointcount and activeflowcount to detect regional problems, then inspect the underlying load balancers and security groups for root cause.. In practical terms, how accelerator metrics reflect endpoint reachability and traffic flows. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

content.html:
Module 12 › Chapter 11.10 › Global Accelerator Metrics
Key metrics
  • HealthyEndpointCount: number of endpoints considered healthy.
  • UnhealthyEndpointCount: number marked unhealthy by checks.
  • BytesIn / BytesOut: accelerator throughput.
  • ActiveFlowCount: concurrent network flows, useful for capacity insight.
Misconception
Global Accelerator indicates endpoint state but does not replace direct checks of ALB/NLB target health or instance metrics. Always inspect resources beneath the accelerator.
Example
If HealthyEndpointCount falls for eu-west-1, check ALB target groups and instance health in that region. Security group rules blocking health-check traffic can also cause endpoints to be marked unhealthy.
Pro-tip
Cross-reference Global Accelerator metrics with CloudWatch metrics of the underlying load balancer for faster root cause identification.
Check your understanding
If ActiveFlowCount is rising but HealthyEndpointCount is stable, what might you investigate? (Answer: capacity constraints on endpoints or traffic spikes.)

screens.title: A reproducible troubleshooting workflow
screens.narratorSegment: A repeatable workflow accelerates resolution across edge services. Start with detection: alerts or dashboards should identify anomalies such as CacheHitRatio drops or UnhealthyEndpointCount increases. Next, investigate by collecting logs and metrics: check CloudWatch trends, CloudFront access logs, Route 53 query logs, and CloudTrail for recent A P I changes. Confirm the hypothesis with targeted tests: run dig/nslookup for DNS, curl requests with varied query strings to reproduce cache misses, or probe the origin directly to see response codes. Remediate with the least disruptive fix first: adjust cache policy, update bucket policy for S3 OAC, change health check path, or temporarily shift traffic using Global Accelerator traffic dials. Finally validate by monitoring the original metric and access logs for recovery. Flow
Detect — alarms on CacheHitRatio, OriginErrorRate, HealthyEndpointCount
Investigate — CloudTrail, access logs, query logs, origin metrics
Confirm — reproduce with curl, dig, or curl with query strings
Remediate — policy change, invalidation, fix bucket policy, adjust health checks
Validate — monitor metrics and logs to ensure recovery
Concrete example
An alarm for CacheHitRatio triggers. Investigate access logs and find many Miss entries with unique query params. Confirm by requesting the resource with and without query params and observing cache behavior. Remediate by reverting cache policy to not forward unnecessary query strings, then validate metric recovery.
Common mistake
Avoid broad changes without reproduction. Replacing endpoints or raising capacity before confirming the fault often misdirects effort and extends downtime.

screens.title: Proactive monitoring, alarms, and dashboards
screens.narratorSegment: Proactive monitoring reduces mean time to detection and limits user impact. Design dashboards that combine CloudFront CacheHitRatio and OriginErrorRate with Route 53 health-check state and Global Accelerator HealthyEndpointCount so you can quickly see whether a problem is caching, origin-side, DNS, or endpoint-related. When creating CloudWatch alarms, set thresholds that reflect normal variance: require multiple datapoints to trigger to avoid reacting to transient spikes. Use composite alarms or SNS filters to orchestrate alerts: for example, fire a critical incident only when CacheHitRatio drops below a threshold and OriginErrorRate rises concurrently. Include CloudTrail-based alerts for unexpected configuration changes, like cache policy alterations or hosted zone changes, because human or automation mistakes often precede incidents. Dashboards should include a short log-search panel or links to the S3 location for access logs so you can pivot to logs fast. Misconception: more alerts equal better coverage — in reality noisy alarms cause fatigue and missed real incidents. Example: create an alarm for CacheHitRatio <= 80% with 3 out of 5 datapoints to reduce false positives. The practical takeaway: invest time in correlated dashboards and tuned alarms to make incident response focused and reliable.

CloudWatch example

  --namespace AWS/CloudFront \

screens.title: Key Concepts
screens.narratorSegment: Let's summarize the essential concepts. First, CloudFront metrics like CacheHitRatio, OriginLatency, and OriginErrorRate are primary signals for cache and origin health; pair them with access logs to find why requests are Hits or Misses. Second, Route 53 health checks and query logs are DNS-level signals; use them to drive failover decisions and to audit resolution patterns. Third, Global Accelerator metrics such as HealthyEndpointCount and ActiveFlowCount help you verify regional endpoint reachability and throughput. Keep in mind that configuration changes are frequent culprits: cache policy changes, OAC/bucket-policy updates, and health-check misconfiguration often precede incidents. A practical habit is to maintain correlated dashboards, tuned alarms, and CloudTrail trails for configuration auditing. When troubleshooting, follow a reproducible workflow: detect with metrics, investigate with logs and checks, confirm with tests, remediate with targeted fixes, and validate recovery. These core ideas make monitoring and troubleshooting of edge services systematic and effective.

fullNarratorScript:
In this lesson you will learn how to gain consistent visibility into AWS edge services and how to diagnose the most common issues. We focus on three pillars: the metrics and logs CloudFront exports to CloudWatch and S3, the DNS health checks and query logs for Route 53, and the endpoint metrics Global Accelerator provides. I will show you what metrics to watch, how to interpret access logs, and the typical misconfigurations that cause stale content, DNS failures, and endpoint outages. You’ll also learn a troubleshooting workflow: detect with a metric alarm, investigate with logs and health checks, confirm with targeted tests, and remediate with configuration changes or cache invalidation. For example, a sudden drop in CloudFront CacheHitRatio usually points to cache-key changes such as forwarding all query strings; the right fix is to adjust cache policies and validate via CloudWatch. By the end you’ll understand which alarms to create, what logs to inspect, and how to prioritize fixes for global user impact. Think about how you would spot an origin error in CloudWatch and what sequence of checks would give you a quick root cause.

These objectives guide our practice with edge service monitoring and troubleshooting. First, you will identify the key metrics for CloudFront, Route 53, and Global Accelerator and know why each matters. For example, CacheHitRatio shows whether CloudFront is serving cached content and HealthyEndpointCount tells you how many endpoints Global Accelerator considers reachable. Second, you will use CloudWatch, CloudTrail, and access logs as an investigative toolkit: set alarms, inspect A P I changes, and parse access logs for request patterns. Third, you will diagnose and resolve common CloudFront issues such as stale content and origin errors by applying cache policy checks, invalidation, and certificate verification. Fourth, you will read Route 53 health check results, query logs, and propagate DNS fixes correctly to restore resolution. Each objective pairs a measurable action with why it matters in production. As you progress you should be able to create alarms, analyze logs, reproduce a cache hit ratio drop, and choose the correct remediation for DNS or endpoint faults. These skills reduce downtime and improve user experience for globally distributed applications.

Continuing the objectives, you'll learn to create dashboards and alarms that correlate metrics across services so incidents are easier to triage. For example, pairing CloudFront OriginLatency with Global Accelerator ActiveFlowCount can reveal whether apparent network slowness is service-side or an origin capacity issue. You will also audit configuration changes using CloudTrail to find who altered a cache policy or DNS record, turning operational suspicion into evidence. Additionally, you'll practice DNS troubleshooting techniques like using dig or nslookup from multiple regions and verifying private hosted zone associations with VPCs. Finally, you’ll implement proactive alerting best practices: set thresholds that avoid noise, choose the right evaluation periods, and use composite alarms when multiple signals indicate degradation. Validation is practical: an exam-style task asks you to identify why stale content is served based on CloudFront minimum TTL vs origin Cache-Control headers and then choose the correct remediation. These objectives ensure you can both detect and act, minimizing impact on global users and restoring service rapidly.

CloudFront exports several metrics to CloudWatch that directly show distribution behavior and performance. Define each metric in simple terms and learn why it matters. Requests counts total viewer traffic and helps you detect traffic spikes. BytesDownloaded shows bandwidth usage and billing impact. CacheHitRatio is the percentage of requests served from edge caches; a low ratio usually means the cache key is too specific or TTLs are too short. OriginLatency measures how long CloudFront waits for content from the origin, pointing to origin performance or network issues. OriginErrorRate and 4xx/5xx error rates indicate failures at the origin or client problems. Concretely, if CacheHitRatio drops from 98% to 40% after a config change, inspect whether query strings or headers were added to the cache key. A common misconception is to blame the origin before checking cache policy — often the policy change is the root cause. Example: a static site that previously served the same asset for all users will begin missing the cache when the distribution starts forwarding all headers. Takeaway: pick a small set of metrics to monitor, set alarms for significant deviations, and pair metric anomalies with access-log inspection to confirm the cause. How will you choose thresholds that signal real problems without noise?

CloudFront access logs provide a detailed record of every request, delivered to an S3 bucket for analysis. Logs include the viewer IP, date/time, HTTP method and URI, status code, bytes transferred, cache result fields like x-edge-result-type and x-edge-response-result-type, referrer, user agent, and TLS details. These fields tell you if an edge returned a Hit or Miss and help correlate user complaints with concrete requests. A practical investigation starts by searching for many Miss entries using Athena or by downloading a sample log to inspect. For example, find lines with x-edge-result-type: Miss and then check the query strings or headers in those requests; if they differ widely, forwarding query strings is a likely cause. A common misunderstanding is to treat all Misses as origin failure; many are simply cache-key mismatches. Here’s an example log excerpt to inspect for Miss entries and query parameters. When you parse logs, group by URI and cache result to spot patterns, then validate cache policy and invalidate if a quick fix is needed. How will you use logs to prove whether a config change or user behavior caused the miss pattern?

Stale content is a frequent issue when CloudFront serves older objects despite the origin being updated. Start by checking the Cache-Control headers from the origin and the CloudFront cache policy. CloudFront respects origin headers unless a distribution's Minimum TTL overrides them; that override is a common cause of stale content. A practical troubleshooting sequence: first, confirm the origin recently updated the object by fetching it directly from the origin. Next, check CloudFront metrics for CacheHitRatio and CloudFront access logs for x-edge-result-type to see if requests are served from cache. If the Minimum TTL is longer than the origin max-age, CloudFront will retain the old object; correction is to lower Minimum TTL or invalidate the object. Invalidations force edge caches to fetch fresh content immediately using the create-invalidation A P I. Use invalidation sparingly because it costs and creates load on the origin. A misconception is to immediately make the bucket public or change the viewer protocol; these rarely fix cache freshness. Example: if Cache-Control: max-age=3600 is set but Minimum TTL is 86400, CloudFront keeps serving the cached object for a day. The takeaway: align origin headers and cache policy, and use invalidation as a controlled remediation.

Origin errors manifest as elevated OriginErrorRate or increased 5xx responses in CloudFront metrics. The practical first step is to correlate CloudFront's error spikes with origin logs — ALB, EC2 or S3 logs — and CloudWatch metrics for the origin. A 5xx spike usually means the origin is failing to respond or returning errors due to application issues or overload. A 403 from an S3 origin is often a permissions or Origin Access Control problem: ensure the CloudFront-generated bucket policy is present and that the bucket is not publicly accessible while allowing CloudFront to fetch. A common misconception is that 403 always means the object is missing; missing objects typically return 404. Instead, 403 indicates access denied. Example: after enabling OAC, you forget to update the S3 bucket policy; CloudFront starts receiving 403s even though objects exist. To fix this, review the bucket policy and ensure the CloudFront OAC identity has read access. Always validate TLS certificates and viewer protocol policy separately if you see HTTPS errors. Ending question: when you see increased OriginErrorRate, what two logs will you inspect first to separate origin failures from edge configuration problems?

Route 53 health checks are fundamental for automated failover and reliable routing. A health check periodically probes an endpoint and reports Healthy or Unhealthy. If a health check flips to Unhealthy, failover or routing decisions may change — so monitor these states and configure thresholds appropriately. In addition to health checks, Route 53 can deliver query logs to CloudWatch or S3; query logs record DNS requests seen by the hosted zone and can reveal querying patterns, sources of resolution failure, or misrouted clients. A practical diagnostic starts with running dig or nslookup from different regions to confirm whether records resolve consistently. If failover does not trigger, verify that the health check targets the correct endpoint, that the request path returns the expected status, and that the thresholds for consecutive failures are not too permissive. A common misconception is that DNS propagation is instantaneous; TTL influences global visibility and can delay changes. Example: a failover didn't trigger because the health check used the wrong path and always returned 200 but with unexpected content; correct the path and adjust thresholds. The takeaway: health checks and query logs together provide both state and transactional evidence for DNS troubleshooting.

Global Accelerator reports metrics that show endpoint health and traffic through the accelerator. HealthyEndpointCount and UnhealthyEndpointCount tell you whether endpoints in an endpoint group are considered reachable; a drop in the healthy count will divert traffic according to your configuration. BytesIn and BytesOut measure throughput across the accelerator, and ActiveFlowCount measures concurrent network flows, which can indicate surge traffic. When you see UnhealthyEndpointCount increasing, check the underlying ALB, NLB, or EC2 health checks and security groups. A common source of problems is a health check configuration mismatch: Global Accelerator relies on the same targets that ALB/NLB use, and if those targets are failing or blocked by security group rules, Global Accelerator will mark endpoints unhealthy. Example: traffic stops reaching Europe because the region's ALB returns unhealthy; the correct next step is to inspect the ALB target health and instance metrics for that region. Misconception: assuming Global Accelerator health alone pinpoints the problem — you must check the resource beneath the accelerator. Takeaway: use HealthyEndpointCount with direct checks on ALBs/NLBs and security groups to restore reachability quickly. Let's summarize the essential concepts. First, CloudFront metrics like CacheHitRatio, OriginLatency, and OriginErrorRate are primary signals for cache and origin health; pair them with access logs to find why requests are Hits or Misses. Second, Route 53 health checks and query logs are DNS-level signals; use them to drive failover decisions and to audit resolution patterns. Third, Global Accelerator metrics such as HealthyEndpointCount and ActiveFlowCount help you verify regional endpoint reachability and throughput. Keep in mind that configuration changes are frequent culprits: cache policy changes, OAC/bucket-policy updates, and health-check misconfiguration often precede incidents. A practical habit is to maintain correlated dashboards, tuned alarms, and CloudTrail trails for configuration auditing. When troubleshooting, follow a reproducible workflow: detect with metrics, investigate with logs and checks, confirm with tests, remediate with targeted fixes, and validate recovery. These core ideas make monitoring and troubleshooting of edge services systematic and effective.

Third, tune alerts and run reproducible tests: change policies carefully, reproduce faults with targeted requests, revert changes, and validate metric recovery.
